AI 或许正在淹没州法院，但要证实这一点又是另一回事

blocks.text: 斯坦福研究人员利用一套基于有据可查的 AI 幻觉案例构建的新基准，来校准检测器，并追踪生成式 AI 在美国四个州法院中的蔓延情况。

inlines.text: 斯坦福研究人员利用一套基于有据可查的 AI 幻觉案例构建的新基准，来校准检测器，并追踪生成式 AI 在美国四个州法院中的蔓延情况。

blocks.text: 自 ChatGPT 发布以来，AI 生成的文本一直在向社会各处渗透：新闻文章、政治演讲，甚至联合国的新闻稿里都出现了它的典型痕迹。许多观察人士指出，法院是一个显而易见、也格外脆弱的机构：事实上，过去三年里，虚假引证不断出现在法庭文书中——出自律师、地方检察官，甚至法官之手。一波 AI 生成的诉讼案件可能让法院不堪重负，浪费法庭的时间和资源，最终使弱势群体无法获得或迟迟得不到司法救济。

blocks.text: 但 AI 辅助在法院里究竟有多普遍？我们又该如何严格地检测法庭文书中的 AI 痕迹？斯坦福以人为本人工智能研究院与监管、评估与治理实验室（RegLab）的研究人员收集并分析了县法院的起诉状，以此探究这个问题。我们发现，AI 辅助起草的迹象从 2022 年的近乎为零，上升到 2026 年受检的圣克拉拉起诉状中的三分之一以上。我们还发现，同一批检测器在不同设置下会给出截然不同的估计结果。

inlines.text: 但 AI 辅助在法院里究竟有多普遍？我们又该如何严格地检测法庭文书中的 AI 痕迹？斯坦福以人为本人工智能研究院与监管、评估与治理实验室（
）的研究人员收集并分析了县法院的起诉状，以此探究这个问题。我们发现，AI 辅助起草的迹象从 2022 年的近乎为零，上升到 2026 年受检的圣克拉拉起诉状中的三分之一以上。我们还发现，同一批检测器在不同设置下会给出截然不同的估计结果。

blocks.text: 为什么检测 AI 很难

inlines.text: 为什么检测 AI 很难

blocks.text: AI 检测这门科学远非完美，在法律领域尤其如此。在我们的新论文《检测异议：记录、校准与检测美国州法院中 AI 辅助文本的兴起》中，我们展示了其中的独特挑战。

inlines.text: AI 检测这门科学远非完美，在法律领域尤其如此。在我们的新论文
《检测异议：记录、校准与检测美国州法院中 AI 辅助文本的兴起》
中，我们展示了其中的独特挑战。

blocks.text: AI 检测器的工作原理是寻找 AI 的典型痕迹（比如“破折号用得太多”）：而在语言使用方式各不相同的领域里，这些痕迹的表现形式也可能不同。法律写作确实与众不同：法律用词比日常语言范围更窄，还充斥着重复的套话模板，留给 AI 检测器的信号因此更少。商用检测器的训练数据也可能并未包含法律写作。

blocks.text: 综合这些因素，我们发现检测率（1）在专业领域尤其糟糕，（2）可能对模型选择高度敏感。例如我们发现，对同一批 2026 年圣克拉拉起诉状，某个 AI 检测器判定为 AI 撰写的比例会随所用设置的不同，从 10% 到 98% 不等。这对所有针对不同细分领域的 AI 检测工作都是一个警示。

blocks.text: 构建基准真相
突破口出现在我们审视一类尤其恶劣的 AI 违规行为时：幻觉和捏造的案例检索。在这些案例中，我们确知 AI 一定被使用过，因为错误实在错得太离谱。事实上，这已经是一个受到严密审视的领域：法律研究员 Damien Charlotin 于 2025 年 4 月建立了Charlotin AI 幻觉案例数据库，专门追踪法官指控或训诫当事人使用虚构引证的案件。

blocks.text: 我们发现，这类案件里充斥着各种新的破绽。现有的 AI 检测工具，比如 Pangram 和 EditLens，要么无法自动识别 AI 生成内容，要么需要大量调校才能用。我们把 Charlotin 的数据库与一套精心设计的对照组结合起来，做成了一个专门检测法庭文书 AI 痕迹的新基准，名为 PhantomDocket。

blocks.text: 此外，我们还开发了一种叫 ScoreMix 的方法，用来校准 AI 检测工具的输出，并统计那些与幻觉文书更相似、而非 ChatGPT 出现之前所写文书的提交占比。两者结合，让我们对法庭文书中的 AI 使用情况得出了经过校准、稳健且偏保守的估计。

blocks.text: 借助这些方法，我们得以较完整地描绘出生成式 AI 进入四个州法院的图景。

inlines.text: 借助这些方法，我们得以较完整地描绘出生成式 AI 进入四个州法院的图景。
到 2026 年，圣克拉拉县和旧金山县（加利福尼亚州）的 AI 使用率分别升至 38% 和 36%（不含债务催收案件）。
不同法院的使用率存在差异。在可比案件中，塔尔萨县和俄克拉何马县（俄克拉何马州）的 AI 使用率明显更低，分别为 17% 和 16%。
自行应诉的当事人（pro se litigants），也就是在法庭上自己代理自己的人，采用率更高。在圣克拉拉，有 AI 使用迹象的自诉状占比从 2024 年的 19% 升至 2026 年的 72%；相比之下，由律师提交的诉状这一占比从 5% 升至 34%。
AI 使用率还因案件类型而异。加利福尼亚州的劳动和商业类诉状使用率最高，而债务催收类诉状几乎见不到 AI 使用——这类文书是模板化的，在某些法院占了近一半的提交量。
AI 使用情况也因法庭文书的不同部分而异，更常出现在事实陈述和诉讼请求部分。

blocks.text: AI 辅助文本正悄然进入法庭，自行应诉者的使用率更高，不同司法辖区的使用率也各不相同。

blocks.text: 基于我们的论文，我们要提醒：AI 检测最可靠的用途是估计总体使用率，而不是精确指出哪份具体文书用了 AI。在我们的基准数据集中，即便是最好的检测工具，假阳性和假阴性率也仍然不低；在语言用法独特的专业领域，直接使用现成检测工具是有风险的。

blocks.text: 我们的研究也提出了切实的问题：AI 究竟是在帮助请不起律师的当事人，还是在让法院被不合格的法律服务淹没？迄今为止，已有超过 1,500 起美国案件被记录存在法律幻觉。这些证据凸显出司法系统有必要正视 AI 在法律行业的兴起。我们主张各法院改进披露政策，以便未来更好地问责和衡量生成式 AI 的辅助使用情况。

AI Might Be Flooding State Court Houses, but Proving It Is Another Matter

inlines.text: AI Might Be Flooding State Court Houses, but Proving It Is Another Matter

blocks.text: Date
November 19, 2026
Topics
Regulation, Policy, GovernanceGenerative AI

blocks.alt: Image 1: Illustration by GPT 6.2 Sol depicting paperwork ascending the courthouse steps

blocks.text: Stanford researchers use a novel benchmark built from documented AI hallucination cases to calibrate detectors and track generative AI’s rise across four U.S. state courts.

inlines.text: Stanford researchers use a novel benchmark built from documented AI hallucination cases to calibrate detectors and track generative AI’s rise across four U.S. state courts.

blocks.text: Since the release of ChatGPT, AI-generated text has been seeping through our society: Its telltale signs have been spotted in news articles, political speeches, and even UN press releases. Many observers have been pointing to the courts as an obvious – and vulnerable – institution: Indeed, over the past three years, fake citations have been showing up in court filings – by lawyers, district attorneys, and even judges. A wave of AI-generated court cases could overwhelm courts, waste court time and resources, and ultimately deny or delay vulnerable individuals’ access to justice.

blocks.text: But how ubiquitous is AI assistance in the courts? And how can we rigorously detect AI in court filings? Researchers with the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI and the Regulation, Evaluation, and Governance Lab (RegLab) tackled this question by collecting and analyzing complaints from county courts. We found signs of AI-assisted drafting rose from near zero in 2022 to more than a third of examined Santa Clara complaints in 2026. We also showed how the same detectors can give starkly different estimates with different settings.

inlines.text: AI assistance in the courts? And how can we rigorously detect AI in court filings? Researchers with the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI and the Regulation, Evaluation, and Governance Lab (

) tackled this question by collecting and analyzing complaints from county courts. We found signs of AI-assisted drafting rose from near zero in 2022 to more than a third of examined Santa Clara complaints in 2026. We also showed how the same detectors can give starkly different estimates with different settings.

blocks.text: Why Detecting AI Is Hard

The science of AI detection is far from perfect, especially in law. In our new paper, Detection Objection: Documenting, Calibrating, and Detecting the Rise of AI-Assisted Text in U.S. State Courts, we show the unique challenges.

blocks.text: AI detectors work by looking for AI’s telltale signs (e.g., “too many em-dashes”): In different domains where language is used differently, these signs may simply show up differently. Indeed, legal writing is distinct: Law uses a narrower vocabulary than general speech and repeated boilerplate patterns, which leave less signal for an AI detector. The training data for commercial detectors also may not have included legal writing.

blocks.text: Put all of these together, and we find that detection rates (1) are especially poor in professional domains, and (2) can be highly sensitive to modeling choices. For example, we find that an AI detector flagged anywhere from 10% to 98% of the same set of 2026 Santa Clara complaints as AI-written, depending on the settings used. This is a cautionary tale for all AI-detection work in different subdomains.

blocks.text: Building Ground Truth

Our breakthrough came when we looked at an area of particularly egregious AI violations: hallucinations and fabricated case lookups. These are cases where we know AI must have been used, because the mistakes are simply so bad. And in fact, this is already an area of intense scrutiny: the Charlotin AI Hallucinations Cases Database wasestablished in April 2025 by legal researcher Damien Charlotin specifically to track cases where judges accuse or admonish parties for using fictitious citations.

Existing AI detectors like Pangram or EditLens both failed to automatically detect AI or needed extensive tuning to function. We put Charlotin’s database together with a carefully crafted set of controls into a new benchmark for AI detection in the courts, called PhantomDocket.

blocks.text: Key Findings: A Third of Cases

inlines.text: Key Findings: A Third of Cases

blocks.text: Using these techniques, we were able to paint a rich portrait of how generative AI has entered four state courts.

inlines.text: Using these techniques, we were able to paint a rich portrait of how generative AI has entered four state courts.
By 2026, the prevalence of AI usage for Santa Clara and San Francisco counties (California) has risen to 38% and 36%, respectively (in non-debt-collection cases).
The prevalence varies across courts. Tulsa and Oklahoma counties (Oklahoma) had noticeably lower AI utilization at 17% and 16%, respectively, for comparable cases.

Pro se litigants, or people who represent themselves at court, show higher adoption rates. In Santa Clara, the share of self-represented complaints showing signs of AI use went from 19% in 2024 to 72% in 2026. In contrast, the share of attorney-filed complaints went from 5% to 34%.

AI utilization varies by case type. Employment and business complaints in California show the highest rates, but there is almost no AI utilization in debt collection complaints, which are templated and comprise nearly half of the filings in some courts.
AI use also varies by section of a court filing, more often appearing in the statement of facts and causes of action.

blocks.text: What the Data Can – and Can’t – Tell Us

inlines.text: What the Data Can – and Can’t – Tell Us

blocks.text: AI-assisted text is creeping into the courts, at higher rates for pro se litigants and at different rates across jurisdictions.

inlines.text: AI-assisted text is creeping into the courts, at higher rates for pro se litigants and at different rates across jurisdictions.

blocks.text: Based on our paper, we caution that AI detection is most reliable for estimating population prevalence, not pinpointing which specific filings used AI. In our benchmark dataset, we show that the false positive and false negative rates remain nontrivial, even for the best detectors, and that using off-the-shelf detectors is risky in professional domains with distinct language usage.

inlines.text: Based on our paper, we caution that AI detection is most reliable for estimating population prevalence, not pinpointing which specific filings used AI. In our benchmark dataset, we show that the false positive and false negative rates remain nontrivial, even for the best detectors, and that using off-the-shelf detectors is risky in professional domains with distinct language usage.

blocks.text: Our research also raises real questions about whether AI is helping litigants who cannot afford attorneys or flooding the courts with inadequate lawyering. To date, over 1,500 U.S. cases have been documented to include legal hallucinations. This evidence underscores the need for the judiciary to grapple with the rise of AI in the legal profession. We argue for better disclosure policies across courts, allowing for better accountability and measurement of generative AI assistance in the future.
